topicName: Metrics, Monitoring, and the Four Golden Signals
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Metrics, Monitoring, and the Four Golden Signals in Microservices"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Microservices architectures distribute application logic across numerous loosely coupled services. While this improves scalability and agility, it introduces significant complexity in observability. Knowing when a system is failing requires robust metrics and monitoring."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The Challenge of Distributed Monitoring"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"In a monolithic application, tracking CPU usage, memory, and simple HTTP response times is usually sufficient. In contrast, microservices involve network hops, distributed transactions, and asynchronous messaging. To maintain system reliability, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) rely on the Four Golden Signals: Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Latency"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Latency measures the time it takes to service a request. It is crucial to distinguish between successful requests and failed requests. A failed request might return very quickly (e.g., an immediate HTTP 500), which can skew average latency calculations downward if not handled correctly."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Traffic"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traffic represents how much demand is placed on your system, usually measured as operations per second, HTTP requests per second, or database transactions per second. Tracking traffic helps you understand capacity trends and sudden spikes."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Errors"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Errors measure the rate of requests that fail. These can be explicit failures (such as HTTP 5xx codes), policy violations (like HTTP 403), or internal exceptions. In microservices, tracking errors across service boundaries requires distributed tracing to isolate the root cause."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Saturation"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Saturation measures how "full" your service is. It highlights the fraction of resources that are constrained, such as CPU utilization, memory usage, thread pool capacity, or database connection limits. Saturation often indicates impending performance degradation."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Metrics with Prometheus and Micrometer"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern microservice frameworks like Spring Boot use Micrometer as a facade to instrument code and expose metrics to scrapers like Prometheus. Below is an example configuration for exposing custom application metrics."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: "health,metrics,prometheus"
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: "order-service""},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Microservice Observability"},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Standardize metric naming conventions across all teams and services."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use percentiles (such as p95 and p99) instead of averages for latency tracking to catch long-tail issues."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement distributed tracing alongside metrics to map out cross-service dependencies."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Set up actionable alerts based on the Four Golden Signals rather than noisy resource-exhaustion metrics."}]
